_comment: Four sample applications used by scripts/run-samples.js to preview the admin digest. STRONG is an obvious yes, BORDERLINE is a judgement call, WEAK is thin, and INJECTION tests that an embedded instruction is delivered as plain text and has no effect. There is no scoring: the admin reads each one and decides.

answers.a1: Development, to me, is the expansion of what people can actually do and choose in their own context — health, agency, time, and the ability to shape decisions that affect them. It is not the same as growth in output. A country can post rising GDP while most of its people lose access to land, water or stable work, and I would not call that development. The test I use is whether the people affected have more real options afterwards than before, and whether they had a say in how it happened.
answers.a2: Development should begin with the people who will live with the outcome, and with the specific problem as they experience it — not with a technology looking for a use. I hold this because I have watched the opposite happen: a solar mini-grid installed in a village near Kisumu where I worked was sized for household lighting because that is what the funder's template assumed. The real constraint was a grain mill that ran on diesel and set the price of milling for three villages. Nobody had asked. Development has to begin where the leverage actually is, and only the people living there can tell you where that is.
answers.a3: Education matters because it builds the capacity to reason, question and act — not just to hold information. A person who can evaluate a claim, understand a contract, or debug a system they did not build has power that a certificate does not give them. Where formal schooling falls short is that it often optimises for examination performance and obedience to a syllabus, and stops precisely where real capability begins: working with uncertainty, forming your own question, disagreeing well. The most valuable learning I have seen happened in an apprenticeship where I was allowed to break things and then explain why they broke.
answers.a4: I want to join CTaDI because the questions I care about — appropriate technology, maintenance, local ownership of energy systems — are ones I can only take so far alone. What I would bring: eight years of hands-on work in off-grid solar and small hydro, including two deployments I designed and one I inherited and repaired; practical knowledge of battery sizing, inverters, and the failure modes nobody puts in the brochure. I would want to contribute to a maintenance-and-repair working group, and I am willing to write up what I have learned about why systems fail after year three, because that knowledge is mostly locked in people's heads and should not be.
answers.b_he1: Off-grid solar systems from 200 W to 12 kW, including battery banks (lead-acid and LiFePO4), MPPT charge controllers, and inverter installation. Small hydro: a 5 kW crossflow turbine I helped rebuild, including the intake screen and the penstock repair. I have done my own wiring, crimping, earthing and load testing. I have also repaired a lot of equipment other people installed badly, which taught me more than the original installs did.
answers.b_he2: A 12 kW hybrid solar system for a rural health clinic in Homa Bay. The constraints were brutal: a fixed donor budget, a roof rated for far less load than we needed, and a supply chain that could not guarantee replacement parts for the inverters we wanted, so I specified a model that a Nairobi supplier actually stocked and could repair. It worked: the clinic's vaccine fridge has not failed since, and they run the maternity lights overnight. What failed was the monitoring — I installed a cloud logger that needed a SIM card subscription the clinic could not afford after the first year, so nobody saw the battery degrading until it was nearly dead. I would do the logging locally next time, on a screen the staff can read.
answers.b_he3: Batteries die first, then the cheap electronics, then the roof mounting after a bad storm. The inverter is rarely the problem. I design for maintenance by keeping the critical spares list short and locally purchasable, labelling every cable, and leaving a written fault-finding sheet in the local language with the clinic or the household. I also try to train at least two people, not one, because the one trained person always eventually moves away. Designing for local ownership means the system should be repairable with the tools that are already in the town, not with a proprietary diagnostic dongle that only I own.
answers.b_he4: I judge appropriateness by asking three things: can it be repaired locally, does it depend on a supply chain that will still exist in five years, and does it shift power towards the people using it or away from them. A technology I would say no to: I was asked to quote for a 'smart' solar water pump with a mobile-app controller and remote diagnostics. It cost three times a basic pump, needed a data plan, and the failure mode was a locked controller with no local override. When it broke, the farmer would be waiting weeks for a technician. A plain pump with a local mechanic would have kept water flowing. The app was solving the installer's problem, not the farmer's.
answers.b_he5: 4. Not a 5 because I have never designed a system above 20 kW and I have not worked on grid-tied interconnection, which is a real gap. As evidence: I independently sized, specified and commissioned the 12 kW clinic system above, including the battery bank and protection, and I have since maintained it for three years. I would happily teach someone to do that, which is why I rate it a 4 rather than a 3.
answers.av1: About six to eight hours a week, mostly evenings and one weekend day. I work full time as a field engineer, so I cannot be available during working hours for calls, but I can do documentation, review and remote advice reliably. I would rather promise six hours and keep it than promise fifteen and disappear.
answers.av2: I would like to start with the maintenance and repair working group, specifically documenting failure modes and writing maintenance sheets that field staff can actually use. Later I would be glad to mentor someone junior on system sizing, but I want to contribute something concrete first.

answers.a1: Development means improving people's lives through technology and economic growth. I think it is about giving people access to modern tools, education and opportunities so they can improve their own situation. It is also about sustainability, so that growth does not damage the environment for future generations.
answers.a2: Development should begin with education and infrastructure, because without these foundations nothing else can take hold. If people are educated and have reliable power and internet, they can build the rest themselves. I think starting at the community level is important, working with local organisations rather than imposing solutions from outside.
answers.a3: Education matters because it gives people knowledge and skills. It is the foundation for everything else — employment, health, civic participation. I think access to education is the most important thing, and technology can help by making learning available to more people, for example through online courses and mobile learning.
answers.a4: I want to join CTaDI because I care about sustainability and I think technology should be used for good. I hope to contribute my software skills, and to learn from other members who have experience in the field. I am particularly interested in data and how it can be used to measure impact.
answers.b_sd1: I use Python and JavaScript mainly, and I have used React, Node.js and PostgreSQL. I also know some AWS. I am comfortable building web applications and APIs. I have recently started learning about data analysis with pandas.
answers.b_sd2: I built a dashboard for a small NGO that showed their project data on a map. It used React and Leaflet and pulled data from a Google Sheet. It was my first real project outside of work. I would probably use a proper database next time instead of a spreadsheet, and write tests, which I did not do.
answers.b_sd3: I think it is important not to over-engineer things. At work we sometimes build custom solutions when an off-the-shelf tool would do. I try to keep things simple, though I have not had many chances to make that decision myself.
answers.b_sd4: Data privacy is very important. I would follow GDPR and make sure data is encrypted and that users consent to their data being used. I would also make sure not to collect more data than necessary.
answers.b_sd5: I would say 3 or 4. I am a competent developer and I can build things on my own, though I still have a lot to learn, especially on the data side. I have not led a large project.
answers.av1: Maybe five hours a week, though it depends on my job. Some weeks I have more time than others. I would like to help where I can.
answers.av2: I am open to anything really. I would like to help with software projects and see where I can add value.

answers.a1: Development is when a country becomes more developed. It means economic growth, better infrastructure and a higher standard of living. Developed countries are the ones with strong economies and technology.
answers.a2: Development should begin at the top, with good governance and strong institutions, because you need a stable foundation before anything else can happen. Governments need to create the right policies and then the private sector can invest.
answers.a3: Education is important because it leads to better jobs and higher incomes. It also helps people participate in democracy. Education is the key to development.
answers.a4: I want to join CTaDI because I am passionate about sustainability and I want to network with like-minded people. I think it would be good for my career and I want to learn more about the field.
answers.b_pa1: I studied political science and I follow policy debates closely. I have written some blog posts about climate policy and I am interested in how regulation works. I have not worked directly in policy yet but I am keen to start.
answers.b_pa2: Politicians and governments hold the power. To change things you need to convince them, or vote them out. Also big corporations have a lot of influence which is a problem. Public pressure can work if enough people care.
answers.b_pa3: I try to explain my point of view calmly and with facts. Usually if you present the evidence people will come around. If they do not, there is not much you can do, so I move on.
answers.b_pa4: I think we need to be realistic and not too pessimistic. Technology will probably solve most of these problems, so we should be optimistic. I do not have a specific example of this.
answers.b_pa5: Probably a 5, because I am a very good communicator and I understand policy issues well from my studies. I am confident I could pick it up quickly.
answers.av1: I can commit a lot of time, maybe 20 hours a week or more, whenever I am needed. I am very flexible.
answers.av2: I am happy to help with anything. I am a quick learner and a team player, so whatever needs doing I can do it.
